title: Parent–Child Play and Media Addiction in Adolescence: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study
authors: Chaeyun Lee, Hye In Jeong, Yeolib Kim
abstract: Although media addiction is a recognized public health concern, the theoretical framework surrounding its longitudinal development remains relatively underdeveloped. This study addresses that gap by evaluating a developmental model that traces a path from early parent–child play at age 6 to adolescent media addiction at age 14, with executive function and peer attachment at age 10 examined as parallel mediators. We used three waves of data from a representative sample of 1,130 parent–child dyads in the Panel Study on Korean Children. Early parent–child play at age 6 significantly predicted higher executive function at age 10, which subsequently predicted lower media addiction at age 14. This indirect path via executive function was statistically significant. Conversely, the indirect effect through peer attachment was not significant, as peer attachment was unrelated to both early play and subsequent media addiction. The direct effect of parent–child play on adolescent media addiction was nonsignificant, demonstrating that the protective influence of early family play operates through cognitive mechanisms rather than social bonds. These findings shift the clinical focus from proximal adolescent factors to early prevention, emphasizing middle childhood as a critical therapeutic window for bolstering executive function to mitigate later media addiction risks.

title: AI-Mediated Mental Health Support: The Role of Attachment Orientation and Psychological Distress
authors: Dorit Hadar Shoval, Elad Refoua, Karny Gigi, Yuval Haber, Inbar Levkovich, Iftach Tsafrir, Ori Pen, Zohar Elyoseph
abstract: General-purpose generative AI (GenAI) models are increasingly serving as quasi-social agents, representing a novel form of informal AI-mediated help-seeking. This study examined associations between adult attachment orientations (Experiences in Close Relationships-Relationship Structures questionnaire), psychological distress (Depression Anxiety Stress Scales–21), and the use of GenAI for mental health support. In a nonprobability sample of 584 Israeli adult GenAI users, 29.3 percent reported having turned to these models at least once for emotional support, coping advice, or mental health assistance; the proportion reached 47.0 percent among those reporting severe distress. These self-reported figures reflect any such contact, from a single exchange to sustained use. Hierarchical logistic regression identified distress as the strongest psychological correlate of use. Younger age and female gender predicted use. Attachment anxiety was associated with use, but this association did not remain significant once distress was included, a pattern consistent with the shared variance between the two constructs. Attachment avoidance was negatively but nonsignificantly associated with use. Findings position general-purpose GenAI as an accessible, low-barrier resource disproportionately used by distressed individuals. The high uptake among severely distressed users (47.0 percent) points to potential safety concerns and to a need for systematic evaluation of the safety, crisis-response quality, and clinical-displacement risks of consumer-facing AI use.

title: The role of democratic values in shaping perceptions of political incivility in European liberal democracies
authors: Sara Bentivegna, Rossella Rega
abstract: This study investigates whether citizens’ perceptions of political incivility converge across liberal democracies and the extent to which individual orientations towards democracy and democratic values are associated with sensitivity to incivility. Drawing on a comparative survey conducted in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom ( N = 3500), it examines the individual factors associated with sensitivity to incivility. The results show that support for democracy and endorsement of democratic values are the most influential predictors of sensitivity to incivility, with higher levels associated with greater sensitivity, whereas anti-political attitudes are associated with lower sensitivity. These findings indicate that sensitivity to incivility is primarily associated with citizens’ orientations towards democracy and its normative principles rather than with national contextual differences. Citizens in Italy, Germany, and the United Kingdom assess incivility in remarkably similar ways, despite differences in electoral systems, media systems, and political cultures.

title: Popular Pornographic Games on Steam
authors: Petri Lankoski
abstract: This study examines which pornographic games are popular on Steam and identifies what players consider to be features of a good pornographic game. The analysis draws on Steam user reviews and genre folk taxonomy drawn from the f95zone database. Game popularity is determined by review scores and counts; these correlate with sales figures, and the combined review counts are used to map genre prevalence and popularity. Steam reviews and genre descriptors are analyzed using structural topic modeling to identify recurring patterns and content themes. The findings show that popular pornographic games on Steam predominantly follow heteronormative pornoscripts, centering male player perspectives and conventional sexual practices. At the same time, a subset of successful games foreground transgressive and taboo content, including monster sex. Across both patterns, pornographic conventions are closely integrated with established game and story conventions, particularly those of narrative-driven genres such as visual novels and role-playing games.

title: Inoculating against fatalistic beliefs: a comparative test of narrative and non-narrative strategies
authors: Minyi Chen, Hye Kyung Kim
abstract: This study compares the effectiveness of narrative and non-narrative inoculation messages in reducing fatalistic beliefs and fostering resistance to conflicting cancer information. A two-phase randomized experiment (N = 572 in Phase 1; n = 332 in Phase 2) tested their effects on counterarguing against attack, cancer fatalism, perceived efficacy, and intentions to adopt cancer risk-reduction behaviors. Compared with control, both inoculation messages reduced cancer fatalism, enhanced perceived efficacy, and increased certain intentions to adopt certain risk-reduction behaviors. Narrative inoculation elicited more counterarguing against attack than the non-narrative counterpart. Inoculation effects also varied by baseline fatalism, functioning therapeutically by immediately reducing initially high fatalism and, more modestly, prophylactically by maintaining initially low fatalism. These findings extend inoculation theory by elucidating the role of message format in sustaining resistance to negative media effects, and by demonstrating the theory’s potential dual prophylactic–therapeutic functionality in a fatalistic belief context.

title: Optimizing Naloxone Education
authors: Huai-yu Chen, Nicky Lewis
abstract: Abstract: Message sensation is commonly used in educational messaging to capture attention, yet its impact on cognitive learning appears paradoxical. Drawing on the Activation Model of Information Exposure and the Limited Capacity Model of Motivated Mediated Message Processing, this study examines how message sensation influences memory and knowledge improvement. An in-person 2 (death imagery: absent vs. present) × 2 (sound effects: absent vs. present) × 2 (animation: talking-head vs. action) between-subjects experiment was conducted among 603 US adults. Path modeling revealed that the need for activation moderated the effects of perceived message sensation on visual encoding and retrieval: as this need decreased, the association between perceived message sensation and memory accuracy (visual encoding and retrieval) shifted from positive to negative. These findings advance media psychology by showing how message features and individual traits interact to shape learning in high-stakes public health contexts.

title: STEM Media Use and Interest Development in Childhood: A Research Note
authors: J. Alex Bonus, Miriam Brinberg, Kate Stewart, Blue Lerner, Julia M. Wilson
abstract: Can viewing educational videos through online streaming platforms (e.g., Netflix and YouTube) foster children’s interest in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM)? To address this question, parents ( N = 338) reported their 2- to 8-year-old children’s naturalistic STEM media use and STEM interests twice over a 1-month period. Children’s baseline STEM media use predicted an increase in their STEM interests over time, with a stronger relationship among older (vs. younger) children. These findings suggest that viewing STEM videos may serve as a catalyst for early STEM interest development, highlighting an important yet overlooked function of educational media use in childhood.

title: Verifying Out of Alarm, or Alarmed After Verification? A Three-Wave Cross-Lagged Analysis of Multidimensional Risk Perceptions and Verification Behavior Amid Climate Misinformation in China
authors: Liang Chen, Xiaoming Liu, Lunrui Fu
abstract: Risk communication research often assumes that heightened risk perception drives subsequent behavioral responses, yet this perception-to-behavior logic remains underexamined. This study differentiates personal-level and societal-level risk perception and investigates their reciprocal associations with verification behavior in the context of climate change misinformation. Using three-wave panel data from China and cross-lagged structural equation modeling, results reveal a clear asymmetry: neither type of risk perception predicted subsequent verification. Instead, verification consistently increased societal risk perception over time, but not personal-level risk perception. These findings challenge the linear perception-to-behavior assumption and highlight a behavior-to-perception feedback pathway.

title: Scrolling for the Truth: Source Factors, Persuasion, and a Test of Misinformation Interventions on TikTok
authors: Brittany N. Shivers Weinstein, Bartosz W. Wojdynski
abstract: The popularity of the video-based social media platform TikTok has rapidly grown in recent years, and with it its role in rapidly disseminating misinformation to its relatively young user base. However, little is known to date about how users perceive misinformation or about how platform interventions could be deployed to stop its spread. Two experiments examined users’ perceptions of TikTok videos making claims about a current health issue (monkeypox). Study 1 tested the impact of information type (true vs. false) and source (journalist vs. influencer) on users’ perceptions of TikTok videos, with party identification as a moderator. Participants rated message credibility and source quality higher for true videos and videos with a journalistic source. Study 2 tested the efficacy of three potential misinformation interventions (a banner label, pre-roll video, and click-through warning) and the role of psychological reactance. There was a main effect of the banner label and public service announcement pre-roll video on perceived message credibility. The interventions had no main effect on source quality, but there was a mediation of the PSA pre-roll and banner label on credibility and quality perceptions through reactance. In both studies, participants had difficulty discerning between true and false claims. Implications for journalists and social media companies are discussed, along with suggestions for future research.

title: Skin Tone as a Visual Cue in Political Campaigns: Evidence from Elections in Mexico
authors: Silvia Téliz, Sandra González-Bailón
abstract: Research has long established that physical appearance and phenotypical traits influence how people evaluate political candidates. Skin color is one of the visual cues the electorate perceives during campaigns and media coverage, and a possible source of prejudice and bias. Here we use computational visual analysis to investigate the association between skin tone and electoral success during the 2024 Mexican Federal Elections. Our analyses incorporate important correlates not considered in prior research, most prominently news coverage, political ads, and social media use. We also account for geographic differences in average skin tone, explicitly modeling a source of variation that is obscured when skin tone is analyzed disregarding contextual baselines. We use fixed effects generalized linear models to control for state and party variation as well as candidate-level demographics, political experience, incumbency status, and media presence (news coverage, political ads, and social media use). Consistent with past work, we find that as candidates’ skin tone becomes darker, their predicted vote share declines. However, news coverage, political ads, and social media use are, together, more important predictors of electoral success than skin tone, indicating that this phenotypical trait is not as prominent a visual cue as earlier research suggested.

title: The Threshold Effect: Preference Falsification Versus Weak Preferences in Russian War Support
authors: Isabelle DeSisto, Grigore Pop-Eleches, Jacob R. Tucker
abstract: How reliable are surveys in autocracies? Using data from wartime Russia, we show why list experiments – commonly used to detect preference falsification – do not always reveal hidden dissent. We identify and test what we call the ‘threshold effect’: respondents may report support for a sensitive item in a direct question but omit it in a list experiment, not because they are lying, but because the list format can create a higher threshold for expressing support. We provide direct evidence of this effect and use two approaches to distinguish preference falsification from weak preferences. Both suggest that outright lying in Russia is limited, but many attitudes are weak and easily shaped by question framing. We conclude that while many Russians genuinely support the war against Ukraine, this support is shallow. Our findings suggest that researchers should take care when designing and interpreting survey questions that measure sensitive attitudes using indirect methods.

title: Partisan differentiation in legislative texts in South Korea: Agenda selection, framing, and partisan classifiability in the 21st national assembly
authors: Sangjoon Ka
abstract: How do parties translate their ideological identities into the language of legislation? This study analyzes 22,964 member-sponsored bills from the Democratic Party of Korea and the People Power Party in the 21st Korean National Assembly, decomposing partisan differences into three dimensions: agenda setting, framing, and partisan classifiability. The study finds significant divergence in topic distributions across parties, with the Democratic Party prioritizing judicial reform and labor rights while the People Power Party emphasizes real estate taxation and regional development. More substantively novel is the evidence for within-topic framing differences: even after agenda composition is held constant, keyword contrasts within shared policy domains reveal recurring asymmetries in problem diagnosis and justificatory language. A text-only classification model further confirms that partisan identity is consistently encoded in legislative texts. These findings indicate that agenda selection and within-topic framing combine to produce a consistent partisan signal. Party discipline, decentralized incentives for position-taking, and ideological polarization constitute plausible institutional and political conditions under which such a pattern may emerge, with broader implications for comparative research on party-centered democracies.

title: A complex arc of engagement: Shifting psychological trajectories of international solidarity during sustained geopolitical conflict
authors: Vivian P. Ta‐Johnson, A. Burcu Bayram
abstract: How do international audiences psychologically engage with prolonged geopolitical conflicts on social media? Drawing on 1.2+ million English‐language tweets posted during the first 10 months of the Russia–Ukraine war, this study examines temporal shifts in engagement, emotion, existential concern, cognition, and psychological distance reflected through language. Results identified a clear psychological arc across the conflict. Discourse in the earliest phase was characterized by strong active engagement, heightened negative emotion, increased focus on death, conflict, and morality, and greater cognitive effort aimed at making sense of unfolding events. As the war persisted, these indicators declined and were replaced by shorter posts, fewer retweets, reduced existential focus, and simpler emotional and cognitive expression, consistent with attention fatigue and chronic crisis adaptation. Unexpectedly, psychological distance decreased over time, suggesting that users expressed themselves in more personal, spontaneous ways as the conflict became an enduring part of the digital environment. This challenges the view that declining engagement signals general disengagement and instead reveals a shift toward more grounded, personally meaningful forms of involvement. Findings illuminate the dynamic psychological processes through which publics respond to sustained conflict and highlight implications for political communication, humanitarian outreach, and crisis messaging strategies across the lifespan of international crises.

title: Bad news for (young) gamers: Using gaming platforms as news sources is more intimately associated with radical belief dispositions than other online spaces
authors: Simon Greipl, Ulrike Schwertberger, Diana Rieger, Brigitte Naderer
abstract: This study explores how digital news use among young Europeans links to radical belief dispositions, particularly within gaming platforms and messengers, where socio‐affective dynamics shape engagement with political information. We argue that online groups are an overlooked locus for biased information processing and the normalization of extremist worldviews. The conflation of an increasingly fragmented online news space with the inherently politicized gaming cosmos can relate to amplified problematic worldviews based on shared activity, identity, and reality. Based on a cross‐country survey ( N = 1489; eight European countries), we compare (the use of) gaming, messenger apps, social media, and traditional media for news in terms of how they afford problematic forms of collectivity, particularly in relation to social, cynical, and radical epistemologies. We find a robust correlation between news use and a set of radical belief dispositions, prominently with messenger apps, but even more so in gaming‐related online environments—less so on social media and none with traditional news use. Notably, a mediation analysis suggests that shared meaning‐making exhibits a negative rather than a positive indirect association with radical belief dispositions. We discuss the complex interplay of how individual factors and platform architectures connect with news engagement utilizing a vulnerability‐affordance framework.

title: Room for Error: Identifying Question Order Effects in Factual Measures When Meaning or Context Shifts
authors: Daniel Goldstein
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology
abstract: Long-running surveys designed to measure trends face a dilemma of prioritization: making improvements and updates to survey items or maintaining consistent instrumentation across survey waves. This includes the order of questions, as researchers have shown that earlier questions in a survey may affect respondents’ answers to later questions, though inconsistent question order across repeated surveys is underdiscussed as an issue for factual items. Primarily theorized to function through the cognitive response process whereby the prior question(s) frames or provides a context for the latter question(s), this phenomenon is known as question order effects. This article examines an example of a clarification order effect in factual questions where reordering the questions reduces confusion and leads to more valid responses. Using data from three surveys conducted in New York City, we examine the impact of question order on estimates of housing unit size. In two surveys where total residential rooms were asked about before bedrooms, paradata indicated increased respondent confusion relative to asking about bedrooms first. In two surveys where the items either had their order reversed or were reformatted to appear closer together, respondents reported more total rooms on average. Qualitative interviewer feedback suggested that when confronted with a question about rooms without other context, respondents often gave the number of bedrooms in their home. They frequently corrected their response after being asked about bedrooms, though not universally. We suggest that this order effect arose because contemporary respondents think more readily about their unit size in terms of bedrooms than rooms. Our analysis motivates our recommendation that questionnaire designers consider question order alignment with background respondent salience as another tool beyond definitions to help comprehension. Lessons indicate that regular and frequent review of survey items, order, and formatting for potential updates can smooth discontinuities and both improve measurement and maintain continuity.

title: ASSESSING THE IMPACT OF VIDEO INTERVIEWING ON MEASUREMENT QUALITY: EVIDENCE FROM AN EXPERIMENTAL STUDY ON MODE EFFECTS
authors: Marc Asensio, Matt Brown, Richard Silverwood, Tim Hanson, Gabriele Durrant
journal_full: Journal of Survey Statistics and Methodology
abstract: Amid declining response rates and rising survey costs, identifying reliable and cost-effective data collection methods is crucial. During the COVID-19 pandemic, major social surveys began to adopt video interviewing as an alternative to in-person data collection. However, its impact on measurement quality remains underexplored. This study addresses this evident gap by comparing mode effects between video, web, and in-person survey modes, using data from the first large-scale experiment where 1,692 respondents aged 20–40 from a nonprobability convenience sample were randomly assigned to one of the three modes. We focus on two key measurement quality indicators: item nonresponse and response distribution. Our results show that video interviews yielded slightly lower item nonresponse levels than in-person interviews, albeit these differences are almost negligible. While measurement differences in responses to survey questions between the interviewer-administered modes were minimal, differences between video and web responses were more apparent, particularly on sensitive items like mental wellbeing and financial difficulties. Our findings suggest that video interviews are comparable to in-person surveys, but they may also suffer from the usual social desirability biases associated to the interviewer presence. Overall, these results are promising and suggest that video interviewing could serve as a valuable complement or alternative to traditional face-to-face surveys.

title: Dyadic: A Scalable Platform for Research on Human–Human and Human–AI Conversation
authors: David M. Markowitz
journal_full: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science
abstract: Conversation is ubiquitous in social life, but the empirical study of this interactive process has been thwarted by tools that are insufficiently modular and unadaptive to researcher needs. To relieve many constraints in conversation research, in the current tutorial, I present an overview and walkthrough of a new tool, Dyadic ( https://www.chatdyadic.com ), a web-based platform for studying human–human and human–artificial intelligence (AI) conversations using text-based or voice-based chats. Dyadic is distinct from other platforms by offering studies with multiple modalities, AI suggestions (e.g., in human–human studies, AI can suggest responses to a participant), live monitoring (e.g., researchers can evaluate chats between communicators in real time), and survey deployment (e.g., Likert-type scales, feeling thermometers, and open-ended text boxes can be sent to humans for in situ evaluations of the interaction), among other consequential features. No coding is required to operate Dyadic directly, and integrations with existing survey and participant-recruitment platforms are offered.

title: Prediction-Based Adaptive Designs for Reducing Wave Nonresponse Rates and Bias in Panel Surveys
authors: John Collins, Saskia Bartholomäus, Tobias Gummer, Bernd Weiß, Christoph Kern
abstract: Machine learning (ML)-based nonresponse prediction in panel surveys enables selective interventions. However, the optimal use of ML predictions in Adaptive Survey Design (ASD) remains uncertain. We propose a method that integrates field experiment results on incentives, questionnaire length, and questionnaire content with ML-based propensity models to simulate ASD strategies ex-post with minimal assumptions. Using German panel data, we show that treating 15 percent of panelists, selected through ML-based predictions and R-indicator analysis, with increased cash incentives or a survey module on the respondents’ preferred topic can reduce nonresponse rates by up to 2 percentage points. These strategies also reduced bias in selected variables. We present our method as a framework for survey researchers to evaluate the expected outcomes of multiple ASD regimes simultaneously in a realistic setting. The framework helps identify both the criteria for allocating treatments to specific participant groups and the most effective modifications to the survey protocol.

title: How Model Choice and Memory Shape Preference Consistency in Large Language Models
authors: Yick Chung
abstract: When a language model answers a sequence of questions, researchers report the model and temperature but rarely what or how it was told about its own earlier answers. I show that this underreported setting behaves as a mode effect. Testing four large language model (LLM) families with revealed preference theory (GARP) across moral, economic, and social tasks ( N = 5,926 ), I find that how prior choices re-enter the prompt, the memory condition , moves the share of internally consistent subjects by up to 48 percentage points, mostly where that share starts lowest. Memory also influences which preferences the models express and, in a silicon-sampling extension, it brings the answers closer to the human distribution. Nonetheless, gains in consistency and surface fidelity do not necessarily translate into representativeness: a consistent, human-looking model may not represent any human population. For LLMs as social-science instruments, this study offers promise, caution, and a method for testing the stability of sequential outputs.

title: Introducing AI to an online petition platform changed outputs but not outcomes
authors: Isabel Corpus, Eric Gilbert, Allison Koenecke, Mor Naaman
abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) writing tools into online platforms raises critical questions about their impact on content production and outcomes. We leverage a unique natural experiment on Change.org, a leading social advocacy platform, to causally investigate the effects of an in-platform ‘write with AI’ tool. To understand the impact of the AI integration, we collected 1.5 million petitions and used a difference-in-differences analysis. Here we show that, at a platform level, in-platform AI access substantially altered the lexical features of petitions and increased petition homogeneity but did not improve petition outcomes. We confirmed that the results were consistent in a separate analysis of repeat petition writers who wrote petitions before and after introduction of the AI tool. The results suggest that while AI writing tools can profoundly reshape online content, their practical utility for improving desired outcomes may be less beneficial than anticipated and introduce unintended consequences such as content homogenization.

title: Algorithm-assisted personalized risk communication to encourage flu vaccination in the USA: three randomized field trials
authors: Gail M. Rosenbaum, Amir Goren, Maheen Shermohammed, Donna M. Wolk, Ann Marie Tice, Joseph J. Doyle, Michelle N. Meyer, Christopher F. Chabris
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare to identify high-risk patients. Laboratory studies are mixed regarding patient attitudes towards AI use. Here we field-tested whether informing patients of their risk for influenza and its complications can serve as an effective behaviour-change intervention to increase vaccination, and whether disclosing AI use in the risk determination or providing personalized reasons for the algorithm’s prediction (a form of explainable AI) influence message effectiveness. We ran three preregistered randomized controlled trials with over 90,000 unique healthcare system patients in the USA (ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT04323137, NCT05009251 and NCT05509283). Patients identified by a previously validated machine learning algorithm as being at high risk for influenza and related complications were randomized to be sent no message or one of several different messages encouraging influenza vaccination (the primary outcome). High-risk nudges increased vaccination: among patients informed of their high risk, vaccination was 1.1–1.4 percentage points (3.3–5.4%) higher than those simply reminded to get a vaccine, and 1.7–3.5 percentage points (3.3–14.7%) higher than non-messaged patients. Vaccination was similar across message arms that did versus did not disclose ‘algorithm’ involvement or its risk explanations, indicating that patients are neither averse to nor appreciative of algorithm use or explainability in this realistic health application. This work was partially funded by the National Institute on Aging of the National Institutes of Health under award number P30AG034532.
